transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-19
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Cobalt CTO), Daniel Park (ML Eng), Roberto Garcia (Head of Infra)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to align on latency/throughput SLOs, measurement approach, and timeline for a POC.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, I'm Maya from Redwood, with Liam our SE, and we wanted to run through what success looks like for the POC around latency and throughput SLs.
[00:12] Priya: hey, thanks Maya, we've got about half an hour ish to go over the goals, Daniel and Roberto are on to cover infra and traffic.
[00:20] Liam: cool, quick agenda — definitions (TTFT vs TPOT), target percentiles (p95/p99), measurement plan, and timeline. then action items.
[00:30] Daniel: sounds good. the big thing for us is tail latency, our users complain when the assistant takes too long to respond. we also care about tokens/sec for cost planning.
[00:40] Roberto: and from infra we need to know peak concurrent sessions, how long requests run, and networking footprints for VPC/nat.

[02:10] Maya: okay first up definitions — we use TTFT = time to first token, which measures how long it takes from request arrival to the first token stitched to the client. TPOT is tokens per second, or effective throughput for generation. we also look at end-to-end *response latency* but TTFT is key for perceived latency.
[02:40] Priya: can you clarify difference between TTFT and overall latency? sometimes we see confusing numbers from other tools.
[02:50] Liam: sure — TTFT is basically how fast you see anything in the stream; overall or TTET (time-to-end-token) is until the full response completes. TPOT here helps us understand how batching or model choice affects token generation speed.

[04:05] Daniel: so for our case — short answers (avg 30 tokens) and some longer summaries (avg 150 tokens). most conversational flows are 2–3 turns.
[04:18] Maya: good — that mix matters. does your traffic have a skew (lots of short vs many long)?
[04:25] Daniel: 70% short (~30 tokens), 30% long (~150). peak concurrency we see ~120 concurrent sessions during business hours, bursts to 400 for promotions.

[06:00] Roberto: on infra we have strict egress rules inside our VPC, and we want to keep PII on prem where possible. so private deployment or dedicated with VPC peering is preferred.
[06:15] Maya: that's fine — we can run POC in Dedicated with a private test VPC to match your network. we'll capture network hop timings as part of the measurement.

[07:10] Liam: moving to SLO targets — tell us what you'd consider acceptable vs ideal. some customers treat p95 TTFT as the key UX metric. others look at p99 for SLA.
[07:25] Priya: our internal bar is p95 perceived latency < 400ms, p99 < 900ms. if we hit p95 < 300ms that's great. is that realistic?
[07:38] Liam: depends on model size and quantization, and caching. for a mid-sized open model on a dedicated A100-style node with batching tuned, p95 TTFT ~250-350ms is plausible for short outputs. p99 will be higher; 800–1,200ms not unusual if cold cache or long context.
[07:58] Daniel: what about TPOT targets? we need steady throughput to hit cost goals.
[08:05] Liam: we usually express TPOT as tokens/sec per GPU and also as user-facing p95 tokens/sec for bursts. for your mix, we can target p95 TPOT >= 30 tokens/sec for short requests; sustained throughput target across the pool would be configured to meet your peak RPS.

[09:45] Priya: walk me through measurement plan: how do we make sure the numbers reflect real usage and not synthetic ideal cases?
[09:55] Liam: good question — recommended approach: 1) use a representative workload from your traffic trace (token length distribution, headers, auth, etc), 2) run both warm-cache and cold-cache tests — warm to reflect steady-state, cold to capture warmup penalties, 3) run tail-focused tests (long duration, steady RPS) to capture p99, 4) include end-to-end network latency by running test harness in same VPC as your app.
[10:30] Maya: we'd also instrument to capture: request arrival time, first byte/time-to-first-token, last token, tokens generated, server-side worker queue times, and GPU utilization.

[11:15] Daniel: how many samples should we run for p99 to be meaningful?
[11:20] Liam: for p99 you want several thousand samples at least; e.g., 5–10k requests across the scenario, or run a multi-hour steady test to capture tail behavior. we'll start with a 1k baseline to validate configuration, then run a 10k ramp to measure p99.

[12:40] Roberto: caching — we have a lot of repeated prefixes in conversations. does Redwood support KV/prefix caching and how does that affect TTFT?
[12:50] Liam: yes, Redwood supports prefix/KV caching; warm cache can massively reduce TTFT because the runtime can avoid recomputation. we'll include both cache-hit and cache-miss cases in the benchmark. also measure hit-rate sensitivity.

[14:10] Priya: what's the plan for concurrency and RPS in the ramp tests?
[14:18] Liam: we'll use your trace to derive target RPS. as a starting point: baseline 50 RPS for 10 minutes, ramp to peak-concurrency equivalent (400 concurrent sessions) over 20 minutes, hold at peak for 10–20 minutes to collect tail metrics.

[15:05] Maya: also we'll collect cost delta for different model variants and quantization — e.g., 4-bit quant vs fp16 — and show throughput/latency tradeoffs.

[16:30] Daniel: one thing we worry about is streaming and client-side stalls. how do you measure perceived TTFT when using streaming?
[16:40] Liam: for streaming, measure time from request to first streamed token arrival at client; we include network egress and client's ingest. we can run a small agent inside your VPC to emulate real client behavior.

[18:00] Priya: ok project timeline?
[18:05] Maya: propose: this week (10/19) we collect traces & confirm SLOs; by 10/22 Redwood shares benchmark scripts and config; week of 10/26 run baseline + ramp tests; 10/30 review results and agree on next iteration.
[18:30] Priya: that timeline works for us.

[19:10] Daniel: what about metrics to include in dashboards?
[19:15] Liam: suggested dashboard: p50/p95/p99 TTFT, p50/p95 TPOT, tokens generated per second per node, request qdepth/queue time, GPU util, error rates, cache hit rate, and cost per 1k requests.

[21:00] Roberto: for the Dedicated POC we need a network diagram and a brief list of IPs; also confirm how logs and audit events are exported.
[21:12] Maya: will include network diagram in security pack; audit logs can be forwarded to your syslog/S3 and we can redact PII.

[22:10] Priya: a question on SLO enforcement — are there built-in fallback policies?
[22:16] Liam: yes — you can configure smart routing and automatic fallback to a cheaper model or different node pool when latency or capacity thresholds are hit; we'll demo that in the next session.

[24:30] Daniel: we also want to test different sequence lengths (context size). will the benchmarks vary a lot for longer contexts?
[24:38] Liam: yes, longer contexts increase memory pressure and may change kernel selection, which affects both TTFT and TPOT. we'll include short, mid, long context buckets in the plan (e.g., 512, 2k, 8k).

[27:05] Priya: picking targets — we think: TTFT p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 800ms as our initial SLOs. TPOT p95 >= 25 tokens/sec for short requests. are those reasonable?
[27:20] Liam: reasonable starting points; we'll validate on the baseline. if we see p95 is 600ms on your model we can look at quantization, batching tweaks, or a smaller model. we should capture cost per 1k responses for each option.

[29:50] Maya: operational question — how long does it take to spin up a dedicated node for the POC?
[29:58] Liam: we can provision a dedicated test pool in 24–48 hours once contracts are signed; for an initial benchmark we can use a hosted/ephemeral pool to get numbers faster but dedicated will give more accurate steady-state behavior.

[31:10] Priya: ok let's try hosted first to get a quick number, then repeat on Dedicated to compare.
[31:20] Maya: agreed — so plan: hosted baseline this week, dedicated run week of 10/26.

[33:00] Daniel: instrumentation — we'll need exported CSVs or a prometheus endpoint.
[33:05] Liam: we'll provide dashboards and raw CSVs; Redwood can export metrics to Prometheus/Grafana or BigQuery depending on your preferences.

[34:25] Roberto: security docs please — network diagram, audit logging retention, KMS integration for keys.
[34:32] Maya: included in pack, we'll send KMS/HSM integration notes and retention options.

[35:55] Priya: final check — success criteria for this POC?
[36:00] Maya: summarize: 1) validate p95/p99 TTFT for your traffic (target p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 800ms), 2) validate TPOT p95 target (>=25 tokens/sec for short requests), 3) provide cost and throughput tradeoff across model variants, 4) demonstrate warm-cache vs cold-cache differences and caching hit-rate sensitivity, 5) confirm network/VPC integration and audit log flows.

[37:20] Daniel: that's clear. we'll sign off internally on those success criteria and share in the next 48 hours.

[38:40] Maya: any other blockers?
[38:45] Roberto: just need the network IPs and a short legal contact for our procurement team later.

[38:50] Maya: I'll include procurement contact in the email.

[40:10] Priya: ok thanks, let's reconvene after the baseline run.
[40:15] Liam: we'll put together the benchmark plan and share the scripts.

[41:00] Maya: recap of next steps verbally: send security pack (Maya), benchmark scripts (Liam), traffic trace (Priya), confirm SLOs (Daniel). schedule baseline run week of 10/26.
[41:20] Priya: got it. thanks everyone.
[41:30] Maya: thanks — talk soon.

[45:50] (call ends)

Notes on measurement specifics (appended):
- Baseline: 1k requests, 70/30 short/long mix, warm-cache run and cold-cache run.
- Ramp: derived RPS from trace, ramp to peak concurrency (400) over 20 min, hold 10–20 min.
- Sampling: aim for 10k total requests for p99 stability.
- Metrics to capture: arrival_ts, first_token_ts, last_token_ts, tokens_generated, server_queue_ms, gpu_util, cache_hit, error_code, client_recv_time.
- SLO targets to validate: TTFT p95 <= 350ms, TTFT p99 <= 800ms, TPOT p95 >= 25 tokens/sec for short requests.
- Reporting: CSV export + Grafana dashboards, cost per 1k responses for each model/quantization setting.

References / links mentioned:
- Security pack (link to be shared)
- Benchmark scripts (Liam to share repo link)
